      The Institutional Determinants of Cost of Capital: three solar projects in Germany and Alberta

      Three fields of solar panels, two countries, one question:
      why does the same sunlight cost more to finance in some places than in others?

      Weesow · GermanyTravers · AlbertaClaresholm · Alberta

      Pick a project and move any input. The model uses the thesis's common-engine equations and reproduces the reported results at the base case: Weesow-Willmersdorf 3.55%, Claresholm 5.66%, Travers 6.23% (post-tax, standalone basis). The swap buttons re-run the one-variable counterfactuals; "Reset all" returns every input to the thesis values. Below the model, twelve interactive charts, including a cash-flow waterfall, compare the three projects side by side: toggle projects, drag points, edit the table and apply sensitivities straight from the charts.

      1. Choose a projectUse the tabs, click a project's bar, or press 1 2 3. The chips in the top bar always show all three WACCs.
      2. Move the inputsEight sliders plus the tax-shield box. Every chart follows at once. Changed values turn amber; R resets everything.
      3. Replay the thesis swapsThe swap buttons re-run the one-variable counterfactuals from Table 6.8 and show the thesis result beside yours.
      4. Work on the chartsDrag dots and white handles, click bars to apply a change or jump to a project, hover for exact figures, and hide or show projects with the coloured buttons.
      5. Present and export⤢ enlarges any chart to fill the screen for your audience; ⤓ saves it as a PNG. Esc closes it.
      6. Keep scenariosThe Scenarios menu saves the current inputs, brings them back with one click, or copies a link that opens this exact scenario.

      “Would you tell me,” said Alice, a little timidly, “why you are painting those roses?”Lewis Carroll, Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, ch. 8

      🔎 The thesis, in this world

      1. 🌹 Three gardens grow roses in the same sunshine. So why does one garden borrow its money much more cheaply than the other two?
      2. 🎨 The price of money: Weesow in Germany pays 3.55%, Claresholm in Alberta 5.66%, Travers in Alberta 6.23%.
      3. 🃏 In Germany the whole palace looks after the garden: steady rules, planned grid, patient banks. In Alberta each gardener must protect their own roses with a contract.
      4. 👑 The moral: don’t paint every garden the same colour. One price of money for every country gets it wrong.

      🔎 The thesis, in this world

      1. 🎓 Research question: how do different ways of running an economy change the cost of money for solar parks?
      2. 📊 Finding: Weesow (Germany) 3.55% < Claresholm (Alberta) 5.66% < Travers (Alberta) 6.23%.
      3. 🧭 Why: Germany absorbs uncertainty through the system; Alberta leaves it to each contract. Both have strong rule of law.

      🐇 The back storySix tiny chapters · tap to open▾

      Before the rabbit hole, there was a long chase. The white rabbit led Maisie across three continents, through a few countries and various field placements, some of them undercover (just kidding… or not). In every industry she asked the same question: what does money cost here, and why? And like Alice, she met a new cast of characters at every turn, each with a different answer. Three continents, a few countries and various field placements later, voilà: a thesis.

      It was never a straight road. She learnt, she failed, and she tried again. There were wrong turns, doors far too small to fit through, and more than a few challenges that felt like the Queen shouting “Off with her head!” Each one taught her something about how money, risk and people fit together.

      🌏✈🌎✈🌍🐇🕳

      It began, as these things do, with a spreadsheet and a white rabbit muttering about discount rates. Maisie followed it down the hole and into her master’s thesis at HWR Berlin: why do three solar parks, one in Germany and two in Alberta, pay such different prices for the money that builds them? At the bottom she landed on twenty linked sheets and a great many tables.

      The tables were far too small to walk through. So, like a bottle labelled DRINK ME, she made them grow: a live financial model, where you move an interest rate and the cost of capital answers back.

      Then the tea party got out of hand. One chart became twelve. The white rabbit moved in for good. Handwritten notes appeared in the margins. The page learned Vietnamese, French and German. A Bloomberg terminal joke sat down at the table, next to the Hatter, and refused to leave.

      “We’re all mad here,” grins the Cheshire Cat, “so nothing here can break.” Wander, change things, and press Reset whenever you want the thesis back.

      P.S. Yes, the rabbit is necessary. “Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be too late!” 🐇

      To everyone who witnessed the chase, who taught her, challenged her, cheered her on, or simply stayed while she fell and got up again: thank you. You are part of this story, and this little universe is yours too.

      With love and gratitude, Maisie 🌸

              Engine conventions

              The rules every project plays by.

              • Horizon 20-year evaluation window for every project; figures in local-currency millions (EUR for Weesow, CAD for Alberta).
              • Rate vintage Weesow priced at 2020 conditions, Travers and Claresholm at 2021 conditions.
              • Generation E(t) = AC capacity × capacity factor × 8,760 × (1 − 0.5%)t−1.
              • Revenue contracted slice at the PPA strike plus a merchant slice at the pool or spot price path; Claresholm's contracted share steps from ~56% to zero after year 8.
              • Operating cost escalated each year with assumed inflation.
              • Debt sized to the lower of target gearing and a target minimum DSCR; interest on the opening balance at the all-in cost of debt; DSCR reported on a straight-line schedule.
              • Tax at the combined corporate rate, after interest and a straight-line capital allowance.
              • Beta one unlevered sector beta of 0.70 for all three projects, re-levered on each project's gearing and tax rate (Hamada).
              • Contracted share moves WACC along each project's modelled slope, about 3 bps per percentage point (Table A.6).

              Limits of the model

              What the numbers can and cannot say.

              • Three projects in two jurisdictions: the results are directional, not universal thresholds for renewable project finance.
              • Leverage risk is priced through a CAPM re-levered beta. Financial distress costs, covenant risk and agency costs of debt are not modelled explicitly.
              • Claresholm's 0.82× minimum DSCR is measured on the straight-line reporting schedule; on the sculpted sizing basis its contracted cash flow supports only about 35.9% gearing.
              • Several inputs are proxies (PPA prices, capacity factors, operating costs, some capital costs) because the originals are undisclosed; each is flagged P in the register so it can be swapped and re-run.
              • Weesow's figure of record is the as-financed Lens 1 build (75% gearing, 3.79% WACC); the 43% standalone Lens 2 build (3.55%) is used only for like-for-like comparison.
              • Current-market repricing uses 9 September 2026 ten-year yields (Bund 3.37%, Government of Canada 3.79%) with ERP and country premium held at base-case values.

              A simplified replica of the common engine (Appendix A, equations 1–13): straight-line debt amortisation, tax floored at zero with no loss carry-forward, a flat PPA price with optional escalation, and LCOE as capex plus discounted operating cost over discounted output. WACC uses the same CAPM, Hamada and tax-shield formulas as the live model, without the contracted-share slope. The thesis presets reproduce each project’s WACC exactly and its LCOE closely (about €63, C$68 and C$69 per MWh); their PPA and merchant prices are proxies, so IRR and NPV will not match the thesis. Treat results as directional, as the thesis does.

                📜 The Rabbit-Hole Charter

                Article I · Entry. Every visitor arrives by falling down the rabbit hole. Nobody is pushed, and nobody is asked for a password in the public universes.

                Article II · Time. The White Rabbit keeps the clock. Every pop-up has his timer, and it always runs out.

                Article III · No beheadings. The Queen of Hearts holds no power here. Every game can be skipped with Esc or ×, and nothing on this site can break.

                Article IV · The doors. The Caterpillar keeps the gates: one sum for the walkthrough, real passwords for the defense rooms, and those stay for Maisie’s professors only.

                Article V · One truth in every universe. The Cheshire Cat may appear and vanish, but the numbers never do: 3.55%, 5.66% and 6.23% on one common model, in every theme.

                Article VI · Prizes. By order of the Dodo, everybody has won, and all must have prizes.

                Article VII · Order. Universes are listed as the books run: Wonderland chapter by chapter, then Through the Looking-Glass.

                Article VIII · Procedure. “Begin at the beginning, and go on till you come to the end: then stop.”
